slides.title: Where are we?
slides.text: Where are we? The topics: Attack surfaces so far... Introduction (in May): Warfare, with an indistinct enemy. Social Engineering (in May): Examples - phishing, vishing, tricking. Human weaknesses. System Complexity: Fight back with design principles, standards and formal methods. Crypto 1: Traditional systems - substitution and permutation. (Pre 1976). Crypto 2: We will continue with cryptography, moving on to asymmetric systems. These systems, combined with modern cryptographic symmetric systems make up the bulk of all encryption based security used on the Internet. We will also look at some of the limitations of those systems. We will look at hash functions, and attacks on them.

slides.title: Symmetric key systems
slides.text: Symmetric key systems sharedkey Alice uses a key to send to Bob, who uses the same key... In this scenario, the key must be distributed to everyone who needs to use it.

slides.title: Asymmetric key systems
slides.text: Asymmetric key systems rsa What if the keys are not the same, and we use public/secret keys? p_{k} is the public key for Bob, s_{k} is his private key. Only Bob can decrypt a message sent to him, but anyone can encrypt it. Participants each have private and public keys, and the keys cannot be derived from each other.

slides.title: Asymmetric encryption and authentication
slides.text: Asymmetric encryption and authentication encrypt PK authenticate PK A model for public/private keys, key rings, many keys... To the left we see Bob encrypting a message to Alice, using Alice's public key. which he keeps on a key ring. Only Alice can decrypt it. To the right we see Bob sending a message that only he could have sent. He uses his own secret key. Anyone can decrypt it, but only Bob could have sent it.

slides.title: Doing both encryption and authentication...
slides.text: Doing both encryption and authentication... badauth goodauth Possible and actual techniques... The technique at the left involves two asymmetric encryptions, and is considered too slow. Instead we hash the encrypted message and encrypt that (much smaller, so faster) hash, to append as a signature for the message. This is what a digital signature is, an encrypted hash, of a file or something. The originator uses their secret key, and anyone who knows the matching public key can check it against the hash of the file.

slides.title: Man-in-the-middle for Public Keys
slides.text: Man-in-the-middle for Public Keys mimpk Motivation for PKI (the Public Key Infrastructure - to see later): We see that a man-in-the-middle can return a bad (public) key to Alice, who incorrectly assumes it is from Bob. From then on she encrypts using a key that Harry made, and who also has the matching secret key.

slides.title: #1: Key Agreement (Diffie (Whitfield) / (Martin) Hellman) [ 1 , ctrl-i2 , ctrl-i6 ]
slides.text: #1: Key Agreement (Diffie (Whitfield) / (Martin) Hellman) [ 1 , ctrl-i2 , ctrl-i6 ] Diffie Whitfield diffie x px Martin Hellman After exchange, knowledge is different... knowledge As explained by Prof Kenochi, the participants exchange the results of calculations. At the end, Alice and Bob can both calculate a new key. Someone listening in however, is unable to calculate the key, unless they are able to solve a computationally complex problem. Each of the participants has a different set of things they know, but only Alice and Bob can compute g^{ab}\bmod p .

slides.title: The construction for Diffie-Hellman KA
slides.text: The construction for Diffie-Hellman KA Concrete: what do the parties do?(modulo math) Alice and Bob pre-determine a choice of p, and a generator g. The protocol is: Alice, Bob choose uniform values a,b from \mathbb{Z}_{p}^{*} and exchange h_{A}=g^{a}\bmod p, h_{B}=g^{b}\bmod p. Alice computes the secret: \boldsymbol{k_{A}=(g^{b}\bmod p)^{a}\bmod p=(g^{b})^{a}\bmod p} Bob computes the secret: \boldsymbol{k_{B}=(g^{a}\bmod p)^{b}\bmod p=(g^{a})^{b}\bmod p} Shared key is: \boldsymbol{k_{A}=k_{B}=(g^{b})^{a}\bmod p=(g^{a})^{b}\bmod p=g^{ab}\bmod p} Abstract: what do the parties do?(\times cyclic group) Alice and Bob pre-determine the choice of group {\cal G} and a generator g. The protocol is: Alice, Bob choose uniform values a,b from {\cal G} and exchange h_{a}=g^{a}, h_{b}=g^{b}. Alice computes the secret: k_{A}=h_{b}^{a} Bob computes the secret: k_{B}=h_{a}^{b} Note that k_{A}=k_{B}=g^{ab}. A common choice of group (as above) is {\cal G}=\mathbb{Z}_{p}^{*}.

slides.title: The OWF (One Way Function) - hard and easy - problem
slides.text: The OWF (One Way Function) - hard and easy - problem Forward function may be done in {\cal O}(r): Bit size Forward Reverse: Discrete logarithm solution 10 10 23 100 100 1,386,282 1,000 1,000 612,700,000,000,000,000,000,000 Relies on doing BIG number maths 1000 bit maths involves numbers with more than 300 decimal digits, but the C “int” (for example) has only 10 or so digits. As a result we need big number libraries. Even with those, to calculate g^{b}\bmod p where g,b and p are large could be very slow, and we need some math tricks. A couple of relevant questions would be Why do we use primes? What is the relevance of Fermat's little theorem?

slides.title: #2: RSA Encryption
slides.text: #2: RSA Encryption Rivest Shamir Adelman rsa RSA is a well known public key encryption technique: RSA (Ron Rivest, Adi Shamir and Leonard Adleman) is a public key system which exploits the difficult problem of trying to find the complete factorization of a large composite integer whose prime factors are not known. RSA can be used for encryption, digital signatures, and even key exchange.

slides.title: 4 processes for public key p_{k} and private key s_{k}
slides.text: 4 processes for public key p_{k} and private key s_{k} Step 1 - create public key p_{k} Select two large primes P and Q. Assign x=(P-1)(Q-1). Choose E relative prime to x. Assign N=P*Q. Then: {p_{k}\mathrm{ is }\left\langle N,E\right\rangle } . Step 2 - create private/secret key s_{k} Choose D: \boldsymbol{D*E\bmod x=1} (i.e. multiplicative inverses). Then: {s_{k}\mathrm{ is }\left\langle N,D\right\rangle } . Step 3 - encoding Pretend m is a number. Calculate {c=m^{E}\bmod N} . Step 4 - decoding Calculate {m=c^{D}\bmod N} .

slides.title: #3: ECC Encryption
slides.text: #3: ECC Encryption ecc ecc ECC Consider addition over cubic elliptic curves, such as y^{2}=x^{3}+ax+b, with zero O, and the points E(a,b)=\{(x_{0},y_{0}),(x_{1},y_{1}),\ldots\} on the curve. The elements are points on a plane not on a number line. An addition operation +_{E(a,b)} for points on this curve: the sum of P+_{E(a,b)}Q is reflection of the intersection R. The group is \left\langle +_{E(a,b)},E(a,b)\right\rangle . ECC uses curves whose elements are finite: prime curves E_{p}(a,b) defined over \mathbb{Z}_{p}, and binary curves E_{2^{m}}(a,b) defined over GF(2^{m}). See the image to the right.

slides.title: Algorithms for ECC cryptography
slides.text: Algorithms for ECC cryptography Step 1 - create private/secret key s_{k} Using an elliptic group E_{p}(a,b), select a point G on the curve which has a large order n. The order of a point is the smallest value n such that n\times G=0. Choose n_{A}:\,n_{A}<n. {s_{k}\mathrm{ is }\left\langle n_{A},E_{p}(a,b),G\right\rangle } . Step 2 - create public key p_{k} Calculate P_{A}=n_{A}\times G. {p_{k}\mathrm{ is }\left\langle P_{A},E_{p}(a,b),G\right\rangle } . Step 3 - encoding using public key p_{k} Choose a random k, and calculate {C=\left\langle c_{1},c_{2}\right\rangle =\left\langle k\times G,m+k\times P_{A}\right\rangle } . Step 4 - decoding using private key s_{k} Note that m+kP_{A}-kGn_{A}=m+kn_{A}G-kGn_{A}=m: {\mathrm{ Calculate }m=c_{2}-c_{1}\times n_{A}} .

slides.title: Why use ECC?
slides.text: Why use ECC? ECC has an embedded OWF problem ECC addition is an analog of modulo multiply, so repeated addition is like modulo exponentiation. We have a “hard” problem, equivalent to the discrete log problem. Consider Q=kP, where Q,P belong to a prime curve... it is “easy” to compute Q given k,P but “hard” to find k given Q,P. This is known as the elliptic curve logarithm problem. Comparable key sizes (in bits) Security Symmetric FFC: DSA IFC: RSA ECC,DH 128 AES-128 3072/256 3072 256 192 AES-192 7680/384 7680 384 256 AES-256 15360/512 15360 512

slides.title: Best attack on ECC so far is Pollard-rho/Floyd!
slides.text: Best attack on ECC so far is Pollard-rho/Floyd! Cycle Trail Want to find k:kP=Q? Cast it as a collision! The world is a chain of elements of the group, partitioned into three (S_{1},S_{2},S_{3}) types (coloured). We either double the element, or add P or Q: {\begin{array}{lll} P_{i+1}=f(P_{i}) & = & \left\{ \begin{array}{lll} P_{i}+P & \mathrm{if} & P_{i}\in S_{1}\\ 2P_{i} & \mathrm{if} & P_{i}\in S_{2}\\ P_{i}+Q & \mathrm{if} & P_{i}\in S_{3} \end{array}\right.\end{array}} Each P_{i} is some sum aP+bQ. On collision, a_{1}P+b_{1}Q=a_{2}P+b_{2}Q, and {\begin{array}{lll} \frac{a_{1}-a_{2}}{b_{2}-b_{1}}P & = & Q\end{array}}

slides.title: Summary...
slides.text: Summary... One way functions an illustration What we just saw were examples based on OWF We saw three systems where we used operations that are easy to do one way, say of {\cal O}(k), and difficult to reverse and do the other way: perhaps {\cal O}(e^{k}), the one-way functions. The Diffie-Hellman key agreement scheme relied on the difficulty of calculating discrete logs. RSA encryption relied on the difficulty of factorization, and ECC relies on the elliptic curve log problem. In each case, we want our mathematical systems to be of fixed size (i.e. modulo), and to operate over all values. A suitable mathematical structure is to use finite cyclic groups, or fields and if you have an interest in cryptography, there is a lot to learn in this area.

slides.title: MD5 and SHA [ ctrl-i4 ]
slides.text: MD5 and SHA [ ctrl-i4 ] MD5... Was designed in 1991 by Ron Rivest (of RSA fame), as a cryptographic hash function. However it has been found to not be collision-resistant (see [i4] above), and so, despite extensive use in industry today, it should no longer be used as a cryptographic hash. The SHA family... Originally designed by NIST in 1993 (SHA-0) but revised in 1995 as SHA-1. Revisions in 2002 led to SHA-2 256/384/512: higher security levels, and with no known weaknesses. SHA-3 was released in 2012 - it is the newest one, with some different design elements. SHA-1 SHA-224 SHA-256 SHA-384 SHA-512 Digest (hash) size (bits) 160 224 256 384 512 Message size <2^{64} <2^{64} <2^{64} <2^{128} <2^{128} Block size (bits) 512 512 512 1024 1024 Number of steps 80 64 64 80 80

slides.title: Cryptographic hashes
slides.text: Cryptographic hashes hash A hash is not just a checksum A cryptographic hash meets extra security requirements. In particular, we want them to be collision resistant (defined on next slide). A cryptographic hash is an important crypto primitive. It is used in digital signatures : hash-and-sign, protecting password files (with salted hashes), Commitment schemes, Proof-of-Work in Bitcoin, IPV6 cryptographic addresses, and so on.

slides.title: Properties of cryptographic hash functions
slides.text: Properties of cryptographic hash functions Desirable properties: It should be efficient, public, and... It should be computationally infeasible to find two items x,x' where x\neq x', but both map to y={\cal H}(x)={\cal H}(x') (collision-resistant). Given x, it should be computationally infeasible to find an x'\neq x such that {\cal H}(x')={\cal H}(x) (target-collision, or second pre-image resistant). Given y, it should be computationally infeasible to find item x mapping to it: y={\cal H}(x) (one-way property, or pre-image resistant). Note that (1) implies (2), and also a (2) attack implies a (1) attack. When two messages map to same hash... Can there be no collisions at all? If the number of messages \#m is greater than the number of hashes \#{\cal H}(\ldots), we have the pigeonhole principle - if there are n roosts for n+1 pigeons... How likely are collisions? Consider the birthday paradox1. What is the probability that at least two of N randomly selected people have the same birthday? It is much more likely than you would suspect... 1 BTW - It is not really a paradox, just counter-intuitive.

slides.title: Time-memory tradeoff ( \sqrt{T},\sqrt{M} ) tables...
slides.text: Time-memory tradeoff ( \sqrt{T},\sqrt{M} ) tables... Idea #1: Precompute chains of values starting from a password guess, and using alternately, a hash function {\cal H}(p), and a reducing function R(h), which generates a predictable plausible guess from the hash. Only store the first and last entries from the chain. It is space efficient, and you can re-compute the intermediate values (a space-time tradeoff). ' rainbowtbl

slides.title: Reversing the hash
slides.text: Reversing the hash rainbowtbl Compute, compare with "last" values, recompute... There is a problem in that collisions may happen frequently... Solution to the problem: the “Rainbow” table Suppose there are k reduce operations and k hash operations in the chain, instead of using the same function R() in all the reduce operations, the Rainbow table uses k different functions. The first reduce is R_{1}(), followed by R_{2}() and so on.

slides.title: The Birthday “Paradox” is not a paradox
slides.text: The Birthday “Paradox” is not a paradox birthdayparadox It is NOT the likelihood that someone shares a specific person's birthday. It is the likelihood that amongst every pair of candidates there will be (at least) one matching pair. This turns out to be quite likely - even here: for N=23 , this likelihood is about 0.5 . We can attack some digital signatures using an attack based on the birthday paradox. Likelihood versus number of random choices In general, in a birthday attack over n items, to achieve a probability of p, we should choose about \sqrt{2n\ln\frac{1}{1-p}} items. In the above, for n=365,p=0.5 we have about 1.177\sqrt{365}\thickapprox22.5. This value (1.177) gives rise to the common approximation we use: take the square root2. 2 For n\mhyphen\mathrm{bit} attack, only need 2^{\frac{n}{2}} values to get 50% chance of success.

slides.title: The birthday attack - straightforward method
slides.text: The birthday attack - straightforward method Find x,x’ s.t. {\cal H}(x)={\cal H}(x’); time {\cal O}(2^{n}), memory {\cal O}(2^{n})... The birthday attack can be used to speedup the search for a hash collision with a “square-root” reduction. Suppose a digest is n bits, and we have a random set of around 2^{\frac{n}{2}} messages (by the birthday attack, the chance of having a collision is around 0.5 probability). A straightforward implementation of a birthday attack stores this set in the memory and then searches for a collision. However, in practice, the memory requirement is more difficult to meet compared to the running time requirement. Imagine if n=80 bits, then there are 2^{40} pairs of messages and digests. Assuming each pair take up 32 bytes, then the total storage is 2^{45} bytes, i.e. 32TB. Nevertheless, 2^{40} hash operations can be done in reasonable time. The following improved birthday attack takes about twice the time, compared to the straightforward implementation, but uses constant memory.

slides.title: Floyd - for chains like x_{0}\rightarrow f(x_{0})\rightarrow f(f(x_{0}))\rightarrow\ldots
slides.text: Floyd - for chains like x_{0}\rightarrow f(x_{0})\rightarrow f(f(x_{0}))\rightarrow\ldots Robert W Floyd Cycle Trail Find loop with f(x)\myeq{\cal H}(x); time {\cal O}(2^{n}), and memory {\cal O}(1) (Robert W.) Floyd's cycle-detection algorithm: the Tortoise t and the Hare h. Variables hop through a graph at different rates, stopping when they collide. Algorithm: part 1 finds the loop in a (digest/hash) chain def H(x): return md5(x.encode('utf-8')).hexdigest() def f(x): return H(x)[:10] def floyd(x0): t = f(x0) h = f(f(x0)) print('Find the loop') while (t != h): t = f(t) h = f(f(h))

slides.title: Floyd - for chains like x_{0}\rightarrow f(x_{0})\rightarrow f(f(x_{0}))\rightarrow\ldots
slides.text: Floyd - for chains like x_{0}\rightarrow f(x_{0})\rightarrow f(f(x_{0}))\rightarrow\ldots Cycle Trail Algorithm: part 2 finds the collision t = x0 print('Find the collision' while (t != h): if (f(t) == f(h)): break t = f(t) h = f(h) if (t != h): temp_t = t temp_h = h pass return temp_t,temp_h This reruns, but just one step at a time. The tortoise restarts at the beginning, and the hare at the result of part 1. They meet at the beginning of the loop (where the collision is).

slides.title: Finding a collision with floyd.py
slides.text: Finding a collision with floyd.py Cycle Trail Run it with a starting point... hugh@comp % python3 floyd.py 42 Find the loop Find the collision Tortoise f375526901 > cfd1d92d5b1d0fcae405b61165d261ed Hare 0eecccc477 > cfd1d92d5bf0b71d1655bc12981bd608 hugh@comp % md5 -s f375526901 MD5 ("f375526901") = cfd1d92d5b1d0fcae405b61165d261ed hugh@comp % md5 -s 0eecccc477 MD5 ("0eecccc477") = cfd1d92d5bf0b71d1655bc12981bd608 hugh@comp % Note that we are only matching the first 10 hex digits of the digest.

slides.title: Practical use in a message/digest collision attack
slides.text: Practical use in a message/digest collision attack Cycle Trail Apply Floyd by using f(x)\myeq{\cal H}(g(x)) Consider messages m\in M, digests h\in H, the functions g:H\rightarrow M, and f:H\rightarrow H defined as f(x)\myeq{\cal H}(g(x)). The elements in the chain/trail of digests are mapped to the messages. Here is an example with good, and bad messages about Bob: \begin{array}{lll} g(0000) & = & \mathrm{Bob~is~a~good~and~honest~worker.}\\ g(0001) & = & \mathrm{Bob~is~a~difficult~and....} \end{array}

slides.title: Code changes for the collision attack
slides.text: Code changes for the collision attack Cycle Trail Algorithm 5.9 for 2^{16} messages in G. Few code changes... G = [m1,m2,m3...] def g(x): return G[int(x[:4],base=16)] def f(x): return H(g(x))[:4] This code only matches the first 4 hex digits of the digest: hugh@comp % python3 floydfile4.py 423485 Tortoise Lord Baltinglas... > e09c3f2d63f7841d33fdbe0bfb4fd444 Hare Tell me more ab... > e09c59046d3b1201931ff649d8b287e8

slides.title: Summary: Crypto-2
slides.text: From Symmetric to Asymmetric...Hash functions Cryptographic hash functionsReversing a hash - the beautiful rainbow tableFinding a hash collision - the birthday attack Summary: Crypto-2 Today, we have seen... An algorithm - We started off this session looking at the Tortoise and Hare algorithm for finding loops in a graph. This underlying algorithm found its way into two of this session's topics. Asymmetric Systems - We saw the asymmetric nature of the keys in cryptography since 1976, and how it could be used for encryption, and authentication. Rather than SPN networks, these systems are based on one-way functions. There were three examples: Diffie-Hellman key agreement, RSA encryption, and ECC encryption. Hashes - Cryptographic hashes are central to a lot of IT security - we use them to verify passwords, to do proof-of-work (say in bitcoin), for digital signatures, and for verifying files. We looked at techniques to “reverse” a hash including the lovely Rainbow table. Hugh Anderson [Q] DADA2026, Cryptography-2 beamer nus logo
